answers.text:
"Computational functionalism" is the specific philosophical position the whole essay is built to argue against, and Seth names it exactly where you selected it: the assumption that consciousness is a matter of computation—more specifically, that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise.

It's worth knowing where this sits in the wider philosophy-of-mind landscape, since the article assumes some familiarity. "Functionalism" more broadly is the older, more general view (associated with Hilary Putnam and others from the 1960s onward) that mental states are defined by what they do — their causal/functional role in taking in inputs and producing outputs — rather than by what they're made of. Its signature idea is "multiple realizability": pain, belief, or a mental state generally could in principle be realized in a brain, a silicon chip, or something stranger, as long as the right functional organization is in place. Computational functionalism narrows this further by specifying that the relevant functional organization just is computation, typically the Turing-style, algorithmic kind that ordinary digital computers run. That narrower claim is what makes the whole idea of a conscious chatbot or conscious silicon brain even coherent to imagine, and Seth flags it as usually an unexamined background assumption rather than something people actually argue for.

The rest of the essay is essentially a sustained challenge to this assumption — Seth's own alternative, sketched later, is closer to Searle's "biological naturalism," which the piece itself explains as the idea that properties of life are necessary, though not necessarily sufficient, for consciousness. So the term you've selected marks the fork in the road: everything from here in the essay is Seth trying to show why betting consciousness on computation alone is shakier than it looks.

answers.asked: This assumption, which philosophers call computational functionalism, is so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all.
answers.text:
This is Seth naming the load-bearing assumption that everything about conscious AI rests on, and the sentence right before it in the same block spells out what that assumption is: the idea that consciousness is a matter of computation — specifically, that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise. "Computational functionalism" is the term of art in philosophy of mind for this position: the view that what matters for having a mind is the functional/computational organization of a system, not what it's made of. On this view, if you ran the right program on silicon, paper tape, or anything else capable of the same computations, you'd get consciousness, because consciousness is (on this view) substrate-independent, like software.

Seth's point about it being "deeply ingrained" is that this isn't usually argued for — it's smuggled in as a background premise. People slide from "AI can compute impressive things" to "AI could therefore be conscious" without noticing they've already assumed consciousness *is* the kind of thing computation can produce. He immediately flags his own stake in the matter: if it's wrong, as I think it may be, then real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with.

This sentence functions as a hinge in the essay: everything before it (the psychological biases, anthropomorphism, the "temptations") explains why we're *inclined* to believe in conscious AI; everything after it (the four arguments in this next section — brains aren't computers, other games in town, life matters, simulation isn't instantiation) is Seth's attempt to actually examine and challenge this assumption rather than let it pass unnoticed, as he says it usually does.

answers.asked: What does "computational functionalism" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
In this piece, computational functionalism is the assumption that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise, and Seth notes this assumption is so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all [spya-wepmnr]. Later he sharpens the term against plain functionalism: functionalism-in-general just holds that mental properties depend on a system's functional organization, whereas computational functionalism is the narrower claim that the organization that matters is specifically computational, usually understood as Turing-style algorithmic computation [spya-f0qxnb].

It matters to the argument because Seth treats it as the load-bearing assumption underneath the whole idea of conscious AI — he writes that the very idea of conscious AI rests on this assumption, and that if it's wrong, real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with [spya-wepmnr]. The essay's central section is then organized as four arguments meant to undermine it: that brains are not computers, that there are "other games in town" besides Turing-style computation, that life itself may matter for consciousness, and that simulation is not instantiation [spya-cv97j7 spya-sk4su6 spya-affgsh spya-e7jqx4 spya-cqh5wq]. He returns to it explicitly at the point of the simulation hypothesis, noting that Nick Bostrom's argument quietly depends on the unexamined assumption that a computer running a suitable program would be conscious — exactly the computational-functionalist premise Seth has spent the essay contesting [spya-xdy4fe]. In his summary, he restates it plainly: computational functionalism — the claim that (algorithmic) computation is sufficient for consciousness — is a very strong assumption that looks increasingly shaky as the differences between brains and standard digital computers come into view [spya-ymbpwn].

My inference is that the term functions as the single hinge of the essay: nearly every other move — the critique of brain-as-computer metaphors, the appeal to biological naturalism, the simulation/instantiation distinction — is aimed at showing this one assumption is unearned rather than self-evident, since Seth says each argument can stand alone but "taken together, they complement and strengthen each other" against it [spya-nv6tp0].

Autopoiesis is the term Seth introduces to name what he thinks makes a neuron (and living systems generally) fundamentally unlike a computer component. He glosses it directly in the text: it comes from the Greek for "self-production," and describes a living thing's capacity to continuously make and remake the very physical stuff it's built from — a cell isn't just processing signals, it's simultaneously manufacturing and repairing its own membranes, organelles, and metabolic machinery in order to keep existing at all. Seth calls this "arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems."

The term isn't Seth's own coinage — it comes from the biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela, who developed it in the 1970s to define what distinguishes living organisms from other self-maintaining systems (like a car's cruise control, or a computer): a living system continually produces and regenerates its own components and boundaries through its own internal processes, rather than having its structure fixed and maintained from outside. Seth is borrowing that biological concept here to make a specific philosophical move: because even a single neuron is "busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence," what a neuron *does* (its function, its outputs) can't be cleanly separated from what it *is* (its material, self-sustaining biology). This sets up his later argument that a silicon chip could never be a "seamless" substitute for a real neuron, because silicon doesn't do this self-producing work — which is one of the four pillars supporting his broader claim that brains aren't computers and consciousness may require actual biological life, not just the right computation.

answers.asked: (This process is called autopoiesis, from the Greek for “self-production.” Autopoiesis is arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems.)
answers.text:
Autopoiesis is a term coined in the early 1970s by the Chilean biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela to capture what they saw as the defining organizational feature of living things: a living system is one that continuously produces and regenerates its own components and its own boundary, using those components to keep producing more of the same. A cell, for instance, builds and repairs its own membrane and metabolic machinery out of materials that its own metabolic machinery generates — it is, in a real sense, manufacturing the very thing that is doing the manufacturing. This is different from a machine, which is built by something external to it and doesn't sustain itself by continually remaking its own parts.

Seth invokes the term at this point in the essay to sharpen the contrast he's drawing between brains and computers. He's just noted that brain activity evolves across multiple interwoven scales, and that even a single neuron is a spectacularly complicated biological machine, busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence. Autopoiesis names that self-maintaining property directly, and Seth treats it as a plausible mark of what separates living matter from silicon — part of the larger case, developed a few paragraphs later, that you cannot cleanly peel "what a neuron does" away from "what a neuron is" the way you can with software and hardware in a digital computer. This sets up his later suggestion, following philosopher John Searle's biological naturalism, that being alive in this self-producing sense might be a precondition for consciousness — something no silicon-based AI, however cleverly programmed, straightforwardly has.

answers.asked: What does "autopoiesis" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
The article defines autopoiesis directly: it is a process by which even a single neuron is "busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence," a process the piece calls autopoiesis, "from the Greek for 'self-production.'" The article adds that "Autopoiesis is arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems" [spya-cf8rt8].

Its role in the argument is twofold:

First, it is part of the case against computational functionalism (argument 1, "Brains Are Not Computers"). Because a neuron is constantly rebuilding the material conditions of its own existence, Seth argues that "brains are the kinds of things for which it is difficult, and likely impossible, to separate what they do from what they are" [spya-zw2m7u] — which undercuts the software/hardware split that makes the brain-as-computer metaphor work in the first place [spya-p4vmm0].

Second, autopoiesis resurfaces in argument 3 ("Life Matters"), where it becomes the material basis he links to prediction-error minimization and hence to conscious experience: "this drive to stay alive… reaches deep into the interior of each cell, into the molecular furnaces of metabolism… a mathematical line can be drawn directly from the self-producing, autopoietic nature of biological material all the way to the Bayesian best-guessing that underpins our perceptual experiences of the world and of the self" [spya-vys3vj]. That line is what supports his tentative biological naturalism — the view that "properties of life are necessary, though not necessarily sufficient, for consciousness" [spya-hj5y6s].

The article doesn't say so, but the term autopoiesis was coined outside this piece by the biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela in the early 1970s to describe self-maintaining, self-producing systems — a lineage Seth is drawing on rather than inventing himself; I haven't run a search to verify the exact date or paper, so treat that attribution as background knowledge rather than a checked fact.
